items.title: Contempt plea filed in Supreme Court challenging 40% job quota in Patna HC for domestic help of judges
items.summary: A contempt of court petition has been filed before the Supreme Court challenging rules under which 40 percent of the sanctioned Regular Mazdoor posts in the Patna High Court can be filled by candidates selected or recommended by the Chief Justice or High Court judges. The petition has alleged that the arrangement violates the Supreme Court’s 2014 judgment in Renu v. District & Sessions Judge, Tis Hazari , which mandated public advertisement and a transparent selection process for appointments to High Courts and subordinate courts. In Renu , the Supreme Court had directed that vacancies in High Courts and subordinate courts must ordinarily be advertised in at least two newspapers, including one vernacular newspaper having wide circulation. It had further held that appointments made without the prescribed advertisement would be void ab initio, except appointments permissible without advertisement, such as compassionate appointments. The plea concerns the Patna High Court Officers and Staff (Recruitment, Appointment, Promotion and Other Conditions of Service and Conduct) Rules, 2021, as amended in July and August this year. items.title: Supreme Court issues 13 directions to tighten bail for foreign nationals in NDPS cases, prevent fake sureties
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday issued thirteen binding directions overhauling how courts across the country verify sureties when granting bail to foreign nationals accused under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act (NDPS Act). The Bench of Justices Sanjay Karol and Augustine George Masih tightened the verification and background checks of such accused as well as the sureties so as to ensure that such accused foreign nationals do not abscond after getting bail. Pertinently, the Court directed that anyone standing surety for a foreign accused will have a lien created on their property equal to the bond amount. items.title: Unsafe food, expired medicines? Karnataka now has a QR code for complaints
items.summary: The Karnataka government on Monday, August 17 launched a QR code-based Integrated Public Grievance Redressal System (IPGRS) to enable citizens to report and track complaints related to food and drug safety violations. Health Minister UT Khader, who unveiled the system, said the IPGRS was the first such initiative in India and had been integrated with the government’s Centre for E-Governance. Under the system, QR codes will be displayed at eateries and drug stores. Citizens can scan the codes to lodge complaints about unhygienic food outlets, expired or overpriced medicines, adverse drug reactions and the use of artificial food colours. “The QR code must be displayed at all the eateries and drug stores. Citizens can scan and register their complaints, if any,” Khader said. The launch comes amid a series of inspections by the Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) across Karnataka, during which officials seized expired, contaminated and otherwise non-compliant food products. Khader said the FSDA would continue inspections and urged the public to support efforts to improve food hygiene. items.title: A Fundamental Right
items.summary: With its new law that makes education a fundamental right with effect from April 1, 2010, India joins a small group of countries with such a statutory provision. All children in the 6 to 14 age group can exercise the right under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009. An estimated one crore children who do not go to school now are expected to benefit.

items.title: ‘Lakhs of eligible voters at risk’: Karnataka groups seek CM Shivakumar’s intervention
items.summary: Several civil society groups in Karnataka have urged Chief Minister DK Shivakumar to intervene in the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, warning that lakhs of eligible voters could be excluded. In a letter dated Monday, August 17, the groups said 1.09 crore voters had been placed in the ASDDO category, comprising those marked Absent, Shifted, Dead, Duplicate and Others. They alleged that nearly half of Bengaluru’s voters could disappear from the electoral rolls, with deletions exceeding 60% in nearly 3,000 polling booths. Elderly people were allegedly being marked as “Dead”, those who had moved for work were being tagged as “Absent”, and voters who made errors while filling out Enumeration Forms were being placed under “Others”.
